https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: LIVERPOOL, England — Nigel Farage will use a speech in a Brexit-backing Labour heartland to start the fightback after Andy Burnham reignited Britain’s EU debate. The Reform UK leader — a key architect of Brexit — will make a “major speech” in Doncaster on Thursday to rail against the Labour prime minister opening the door to a possible return to the bloc, a senior Reform official told POLITICO. Burnham used his first Labour conference as leader, in Liverpool on Tuesday, to snip three political livewires in British politics, including proposing a change to the “triple lock” protecting the state pension and electoral reform. Advertisement Advertisement Farage is spoiling to address all these fault-lines on Thursday. “He will talk about Burnham wanting to take us into the Euro, return us to freedom of movement with 500 million people and losing the ability to nationalize key industries,” said the Reform official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the pending speech in Doncaster. The Yorkshire city voted 69% in favor of leaving the EU in the 2016 referendum, making it one of the most pro-Brexit areas in the U.K. One of its MPs is Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. Burnham has reopened the debate in Labour and beyond by saying he will canvass opinion on several options for Britain’s future arrangement with Brussels and set them out around the time of a EU-U.K. summit later this year. Those options, he has said, could include rejoining the single market, the customs union, or “go all the way,” which Reform is interpreting as scrapping the Pound in favor of the Euro. Burnham has not made that specific pledge, and Labour resisted Britain joining the single currency when it was introduced. Farage is meanwhile planning to argue that EU re-entry would curb the ability of British governments to nationalize key industries — a play by the Reform leader that upends the traditional left-right debate in British politics. Burnham has put emphasis on bringing back “public control” of privatized utilities rather than public ownership, but Farage has changed tack from his Thatcherite credentials to express support for nationalization in some sectors. Advertisement Advertisement So far most of Farage’s criticism of Burnham’s speech has centered on accusing Labour of “going after pensioners” on the triple lock. But his stance on the PM announcing a commission to investigate overhauling Britain’s first-past-the-post electoral system will be one to watch. The current voting system makes it incredibly hard for insurgent parties, like Reform, to get a foothold in Parliament. But after a certain polling threshold is crossed it rewards parties with vast numbers of seats on proportionally little of the vote. Farage has long been in favor of changing this system — but his party has recently attacked Labour’s reversion to a more proportional voting system in mayoral races as being an “establishment stitch-up.”

Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters View image in fullscreen Donald Trump and his allies have called for US representative Ilhan Omar to be expelled from the US. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Democratic leaders condemn federal raid on Ilhan Omar as she vows not to be silenced Minnesota congresswoman criticized raid as attempt by Trump administration ‘to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement’. Plus what is to be done about the world record in the women’s marathon? Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Martin Belam Tue 13 Oct 2026 06.55 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Ilhan Omar has said she will not be silenced after federal agents raided her home. In a social media post, the Minnesota congresswoman criticized the raid as an attempt by the Trump administration “to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement”. Donald Trump and key allies have accused Omar of fraud related to her family’s immigration history, fantasizing openly about denaturalizing her and expelling her from the country. Omar said in her post: “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” How have Ilhan Omar’s Democratic colleagues reacted to the raid? House Democratic leaders, including the minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, the party whip, Katherine Clark and caucus chair, Pete Aguilar, issued a joint statement excoriating the president for the search, calling it “deeply disturbing”. The Democratic leaders vowed to “deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power” from the US Departments of Justice and Homeland Security. Mamdani says ICE agents who shot man in New York looked like ‘mass shooters’ View image in fullscreen Zohran Mamdani. Photograph: Seth Wenig/AP The New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, compared US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) recent shooting of a man in Manhattan to a mass shooting scene – and called for an end to the agency’s operations in his city. Oscar Belgal, 28, was struck in the neck during an enforcement operation while he was in his car with his five-year-old child also inside. Describing his perspective on videos of the shooting scene that have emerged since, Mamdani told MS NOW it was unclear even to the mayor that the agents in the footage were law enforcement personnel based on their being in plainclothes. Federal judge orders temporary halt to taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads View image in fullscreen The ads promoted the president ahead of the midterm elections. Photograph: Ron Sachs/EPA A federal judge has ordered Donald Trump’s administration to temporarily halt the broadcast of taxpayer-funded television ads promoting the president ahead of the 3 November midterm elections. A temporary restraining order aimed at the ads is meant to stay in effect for at least 14 days. The administration “shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the … advertisements,” the judge said in her ruling. She also ordered the administration to cancel the remaining portion of a $20m advertising purchase, halting further spending on the campaign. Anti-vaxxers target Texas measles doctors to cast doubt on deaths amid outbreak View image in fullscreen An MMR vaccine being prepared. Photograph: Mary Conlon/AP Amid rising measles outbreaks and fatalities across the US, anti-vaccine activists – including figures such as the HHS secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and Children’s Health Defense – are actively working to dispute official death tolls and cast doubt on the virus’s severity. To deflect accountability for the resurgence of preventable disease, these groups are promoting claims that patient deaths stem from medical error and inappropriate treatment rather than measles complications, even filing formal medical board complaints against treating pediatricians. Public health experts and physicians warn that this playbook fuels distrust, vilifies frontline healthcare workers, and distracts from the core issue of declining vaccination rates Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’ View image in fullscreen Cocaine hidden in a ship off Spain’s Canary Islands. Photograph: Policía Nacional A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe , where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations. The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe and does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias. In other news … View image in fullscreen RJ Mitte played Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian RJ Mitte, the actor best known for Breaking Bad, has died aged 34 . Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr in the show, took his own life in Brownsville, Texas. The archbishop of Catholics in the US military has condemned Pentagon plans to livestream an execution , and says Catholics on the army firing squad should ask to be excused, since it clashes with church teachings. Theme park company Six Flags temporarily closed nine rollercoasters across six amusement parks after one person died. Several others were injured in an incident involving a coaster in Georgia. About 70 runners participating in Utah’s Moab 240 ultramarathon were successfully evacuated after being stranded by flooding stemming from the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel. Qantas has been forced to ground a plane in Rome after bedbugs were discovered on the aircraft on its way from Perth. Stat of the day: Michael Jordan Last Dance jersey bought for record $14m in private sale View image in fullscreen Chicago Bulls’ Michael Jordan. Photograph: Mark J Terrill/AP A jersey worn by Michael Jordan during the 1998 NBA finals has been sold for $14m in what is said to be the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia. Culture pick: Below review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh Hartnett View image in fullscreen Josh Hartnett as Calvin in Below. Photograph: Netflix/PA Don your best plaid shirts for this Netflix supernatural thriller about a gang of beefy fishers who tackle sea monsters. It is totally ridiculous – but Sarah Dempster says you will have loads of daft fun. Don’t miss this: Fraternities are the most likely place for unwanted sexual contact – should they be shut down? View image in fullscreen Cornell University students hold protest signs. Photograph: Angelina Katsanis/Reuters As an alleged 2024 gang-rape at Cornell comes to light, Eric Berger reports that US universities are grappling with a choice: student safety or alumni donations. … or this: Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done? View image in fullscreen Ruth Chepngetich of Kenya. Photograph: Patrick Gorski/USA Today Sports Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act. Sean Ingle has spoken to Brett Clothier, the head of the Athletics Integrity Unit, which prosecuted the case against Chepngetich. Climate check: IPCC is under pressure to delay publication of key global climate report View image in fullscreen Ceylon spotted deer drink from a water hole that has shrunk due to a drought in Sri Lanka. Photograph: Eranga Jayawardena/AP In this analysis piece , our environment editor, Fiona Harvey, examines how some petro-states and major developing countries want to postpone one of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s key reports. Last Thing: Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearance View image in fullscreen Amelia Earhart. Photograph: Albert Bresnik/AP Researchers will head to a remote Pacific atoll where they suspect the famed aviator Amelia Earhart crash-landed in 1937, but sceptics say the satellite images that have inspired the trip are unlikely to be of her aircraft. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting at the Constantine Palace in St Petersburg. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/State Media Handout/Reuters View image in fullscreen Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin shake hands during a meeting at the Constantine Palace in St Petersburg. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/State Media Handout/Reuters Russia Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks Russia frees Stephen Hubbard after US request while Steve Witkoff praises Putin, wanted by ICC as war criminal, as a ‘humanitarian’ Europe live – latest updates US politics live – latest updates Pjotr Sauer Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.24 EDT First published on Wed 21 Oct 2026 07.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington. Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine . His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine , while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections. Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia , rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country. Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week. He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.” View image in fullscreen Stephen Hubbard in court in Moscow in October 2024. Photograph: Moscow city court press service/AP Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US. The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war. More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher. The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace. Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year. Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.” The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war. View image in fullscreen ‘You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,’ Witkoff told Putin during their meeting. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries. Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield , the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network. Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House. ‘Drones all night. By morning, you smell the smoke’: life in the last hotel on Ukraine’s frontline Read more During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”. Witkoff said there was “some degree of momentum” behind efforts to reach a peace deal, describing the talks in Oslo as “constructive”. Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv. The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region. After the Witkoff meeting, the Kremlin said it was open to new three-way peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and US, which could take place ⁠in Abu Dhabi and would be focused on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended. Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market. Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes. Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze. The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders. https://www.bursa.ro/schools-under-assau.text: Schools across several parts of Europe are facing a literal, violent assault. From grievances regarding the education system to clashes with police and attacks committed within school grounds, several European nations are confronting episodes of youth violence. Authorities in two areas have been placed on high alert. Student protests in France and recent attacks in Polish schools have once again highlighted an issue that transcends national borders: the increasingly strained relationship between a segment of the younger generation and the institutions, authority figures, and social environments that shape them. In France, demonstrations were sparked by dissatisfaction with educational conditions, teacher shortages, and the state of school infrastructure, Reuters reports. In some cities, protests escalated into arson, vandalism, and clashes with law enforcement. Meanwhile, in Poland, three attacks within educational institutions over the span of four days resulted in one death and injuries to several people-including children-according to the AP. The two situations are not equivalent. France is witnessing a protest movement driven by educational and social demands, whereas in Poland, authorities are investigating acts of individual aggression-incidents Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggests were influenced by the online glorification of violence. Nevertheless, both cases illustrate the challenges institutions face in managing tensions involving young people and minors. *France: School-related grievances spill onto the streets According to Reuters, protests by French students intensified; on October 8, the Ministry of the Interior estimated nationwide turnout at 71,500 people, with 24,500 in Paris alone. Now in its third week, the movement was sparked by dissatisfaction with educational conditions and has spread from the capital region to other urban centers. Demands include smaller class sizes, the filling of vacant teaching positions, improvements to school facilities, and changes to the curriculum. Students have also denounced inequalities within the education system and police violence. Reuters reports that while demonstrations in Paris were largely peaceful, serious incidents occurred elsewhere. In Bordeaux, rioters attacked a police station; a school in Saint-Étienne was trashed; and teachers in Toulouse and Marseille were assaulted during the protests. French authorities thus face a dual challenge: they must address grievances regarding the functioning of the education system while also preventing the demonstrations from escalating into street violence. French media reports indicate that the large-scale mobilization was accompanied by police interventions, arrests, and injuries among participants. In some instances, the police response itself became a focal point of the protests, fueling tensions between demonstrators and the authorities. *Poland: Three Attacks in Four Days In Poland, the situation has taken a much more serious turn due to attacks carried out at educational institutions. According to the Associated Press (AP), three incidents occurred in the central province of Mazovia over the course of four days. A 19-year-old vocational school student injured nine people with a sharp object. In another case, a 15-year-old attacked staff at his former primary school, killing a caretaker and injuring two others. On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman injured three people at a post-secondary educational institution in Warsaw. Following these incidents, authorities stepped up security checks. By Sunday morning, police had detained 117 individuals for possessing knives or other dangerous objects, or for making threats regarding attacks on schools and fellow students. Approximately 64,000 schools were inspected, according to data provided by the AP. Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that the attacks do not appear to be part of a large-scale organized operation, but rather spontaneous acts inspired by online content. The Polish leader warned of a growing fascination with violence and an interest among some young people in extremist ideologies, Nazi symbols, and individuals who have committed mass attacks and subsequently been glorified on the internet. *Social Media and the Risk of Copycat Attacks One of the main concerns of Polish authorities is the possibility that acts of aggression might be imitated by other young people who follow reports on the attacks or consume online content portraying the perpetrators as role models. The AP quotes Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center. Counter-Terrorism [center] in The Hague, which drew attention to the similarities between symbols used by one of the Polish suspects and those associated with Brenton Tarrant-the perpetrator of the 2019 attacks on two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, that left 51 people dead. While these similarities do not in themselves prove the existence of an organized network, they raise the issue of how extremist symbols circulate and how certain criminals are transformed into figures admired within specific online communities. Donald Tusk described the situation as a phenomenon with broader social and cultural implications. He urged parents and teachers to discuss online activity with young people and to address the consequences of participating in communities that glorify aggression. The Polish government also announced plans to renew efforts to restrict access to online content deemed harmful to minors. According to the AP, Tusk argued that authorities currently lack all the legal tools they consider necessary to block such material. *Two different crises, a shared challenge regarding prevention Any comparison between France and Poland must be made without conflating social protest with criminal violence. French students demanding teachers, decent learning conditions, and a more equitable education system cannot be equated with those who commit attacks against classmates or teachers. Nor do violent incidents occurring during demonstrations justify attributing extreme behaviors to the protest movement as a whole. However, a common question faces the authorities: how can tensions be identified and managed before they escalate into acts of aggression? In France, protests have brought to light long-standing grievances within schools and the challenges facing the education system. In Poland, attacks have highlighted the risks associated with online threats, the spread of extremist symbols, and the potential for copycat behavior. In both instances, the institutional response cannot be limited to police intervention and security measures, however necessary these may be in situations of immediate danger. Schools play a vital role not only in imparting knowledge but also in shaping social behavior. When students feel their concerns are not being heard, tensions can escalate. At the same time, exposure to violent and extremist content creates risks that require specific interventions-not only from families and teachers but also from the institutions responsible for public safety. Events in both countries demonstrate the limitations of a purely punitive approach. While security measures can prevent certain incidents and investigations can identify those responsible, long-term prevention requires an understanding of the root causes that foster violence. In France, authorities must address the specific issues raised by students without allowing demonstrations to become a pretext for aggression and destruction. In Poland, the immediate priority is to protect students and school staff while simultaneously investigating the attacks and any potential links to online extremist circles. There also remains the issue of the responsibility of digital platforms, through which violent imagery, threats, and extremist symbols can spread rapidly. However, combating this phenomenon requires well-founded measures that protect minors without turning any nonconformist behavior or protest into grounds for suspicion.
